title: Acme AI releases a local coding assistant with repository-scoped access
text: Acme AI released a coding assistant named Workshop on Wednesday. The assistant runs on a developer's own computer and can inspect only repositories that the developer explicitly selects. The release includes support for Python and JavaScript projects. It is not a general-purpose computer agent, and it cannot browse unrelated folders. Developers can ask it to explain a function, propose a patch, or identify tests relevant to a change. Proposed edits appear in a review screen before they are applied. The initial release does not execute terminal commands automatically. A developer must approve each test command separately. Acme says these restrictions are intended to make the assistant practical for teams handling proprietary code. Workshop records the files it read and the commands it requested in a local audit log. That log can be deleted by the operator and is not uploaded by default. An optional team feature lets administrators distribute shared repository policies. The company evaluated the tool on a published collection of 120 small maintenance tasks, reporting successful patches on 78 of them. Those results were measured by Acme rather than an independent testing organization. Acme has released the task descriptions and test commands so other developers can reproduce the evaluation. The company did not publish a comparison against every competing assistant. The free version handles one repository at a time. A paid team edition is planned, but Acme has not announced its price or release date. Linux and macOS are supported at launch; Windows support remains under development. Acme recommends starting with a disposable branch and reviewing every proposed edit. The release notes also warn that generated explanations can be wrong, even when the proposed patch passes existing tests. The next planned update will add a way to export audit records for code review.

title: Apple publishes a Swift package signing preview for developers
text: Apple published a developer preview of a package-signing workflow for Swift projects on Wednesday. The preview lets a package maintainer attach a signature to a release and lets a consuming project verify that signature during dependency resolution. The workflow is available in a preview command-line toolchain, not the stable toolchain distributed with the current Xcode release. Developers must opt in for each project. Existing unsigned dependencies continue to work when verification is not enabled. Apple says the preview is intended to gather feedback about distributing signing keys and recovering from a compromised key. The first version supports a list of trusted keys stored with the consuming project's configuration. When verification is enabled, a package release signed with an unknown key is rejected until a developer updates that list. A signature establishes which key signed the release; it does not establish that the package is free of security flaws. The documentation makes that distinction explicit and recommends continuing normal dependency review and automated testing. Package maintainers can sign a new release without changing their source code. Consumers can also inspect a verification report showing the package version, signer, and verification result. The preview does not automatically replace a dependency with a different version when verification fails. It stops resolution and reports the failure instead. Apple has published examples for both a small library and a workspace with several packages. The company is asking maintainers to report problems with key rotation, build caches, and continuous integration systems. No date has been announced for making the workflow part of the stable toolchain or for requiring signatures across the package ecosystem. Developers evaluating the preview are advised to use a separate branch and retain their existing lockfile. The proposal will be revised after the first round of public feedback.

title: Bills move Wednesday practice indoors and revise offensive-line rotations
text: The Buffalo Bills moved Wednesday's practice indoors because of thunderstorms near the training facility. The change affected the practice location but did not cancel the session. Coaches used the workout to give the second-team offensive line additional repetitions in protection drills. The head coach said the rotation was part of the team's preparation for its next preseason game, not an announcement of the starting lineup. The team has not finalized that lineup. During the portion of practice open to reporters, the offense worked on communication against simulated pressure from several defensive formations. The drills emphasized identifying the pass rusher and passing off assignments between adjacent linemen. Coaches stopped several plays to repeat the communication calls before restarting the drill. Two players who had been limited earlier in the week participated in individual exercises but did not join the full team period. The Bills did not announce a new injury diagnosis or a return date for either player. The coaching staff said participation would be reviewed again before the next practice. The starting quarterback took part in the scheduled team periods. Backup quarterbacks also received repetitions with different offensive-line combinations. A team spokesperson said the indoor move did not change the planned length of the workout. The public portion of the next scheduled practice remains subject to weather conditions, and the team will publish any change through its normal announcement channels. Coaches plan to review the practice film before deciding which combinations receive additional work in the next session. The head coach cautioned against treating one day's rotation as a depth-chart decision. He said the evaluation includes assignments, communication, and consistency across several practices. The team did not announce a trade, a roster cut, or a change to its upcoming game schedule.
